articles.title: Secrecy Is Killing Data Center Deals
articles.narrative: The data center industry's reliance on secrecy, through non-disclosure agreements and redacted filings, is causing significant project delays and cancellations due to community opposition. This lack of transparency, often justified as protecting proprietary information, backfires by eroding trust and fueling resistance when communities feel excluded from key decisions. The author argues that transparency should be viewed as a strategic development tool, not a concession, as early and consistent disclosure of foundational information like power demand, water use, and site plans leads to smoother approvals and fewer challenges. The current fragmented disclosure practices create an environment of resistance and risk for developers, highlighting the need for a standardized framework to ensure projects are evaluated on their merits rather than rejected on principle.

articles.title: Stephen Wendell of Mountain Shore Properties: 5 Questions
articles.narrative: This article is a Q&A interview with Stephen Wendell, CEO of Mountain Shore Properties, discussing the firm's history, diversified portfolio, and development strategy. Mountain Shore Properties, founded by Wendell's father in the 1980s, has grown into a national real estate development company with over $400 million in project value, focusing on hospitality, residential, and office properties across more than 25 cities in 11 states. Wendell emphasizes the firm's intentional diversification across asset classes and geographies, with a particular focus on hotel development, often leveraging existing market knowledge from previous projects to expand into other asset types.

articles.title: Land Use Intelligence Is Increasingly a Must-Have in Deal-Making
articles.narrative: This article argues that land use intelligence, particularly zoning data, must be integrated earlier into the commercial real estate underwriting process to mitigate costly mistakes. The author contends that while financial models are sophisticated, underlying assumptions about property characteristics and local regulations often lead to errors because zoning information is fragmented and traditionally treated as a downstream diligence item. By leveraging new technology and AI to centralize and connect land use data with other datasets, investors, developers, and lenders can make more informed decisions, identify risks sooner, and improve deal outcomes.

articles.title: Housing Notes: Inman tells Compass to pound sand
articles.narrative: This opinion piece praises Inman News for resisting pressure from Compass to remove an op-ed by Bess Freedman, CEO of Brown Harris Stevens. Freedman's article criticized Compass's alleged practice of steering sellers into 90-day private listing periods, arguing that this boosts Compass's internal economics while limiting market exposure and potentially depressing sale prices. The author supports Freedman's claims, suggesting that such practices violate fiduciary and fair housing obligations and reduce transparency. The article highlights that New York's Attorney General has initiated an antitrust investigation into Compass, and proposed state legislation aims to restrict private listings to protect consumers.

articles.title: The Data Drop: The profitability of rent-stabilized buildings
articles.narrative: This article from The Data Drop by TRD Data presents a weekly look at real estate numbers, focusing on several key market trends. It examines the profitability of rent-stabilized buildings in NYC, finding that even those with numerous housing code violations can still be profitable, despite some limitations in the data. The report also highlights that most NYC home sellers profited in 2025, with Manhattan being an exception due to its condo boom. Additionally, home flipping has declined across NYC and the state, coinciding with proposed legislation for a new tax on flippers. Finally, the article notes a significant housing boom in northern Collin County, Texas, particularly in Celina, driven by infrastructure development and population growth.

articles.title: Blackstone's QTS Abandons Digital Gateway Project, Ends Legal Fight
articles.narrative: Blackstone's data center arm, QTS, has officially withdrawn from the ambitious Digital Gateway project in Prince William County, Virginia, and ceased its legal battle to advance the development. This decision follows a lower court ruling that voided the necessary rezoning approvals, and the company determined that further litigation was not worthwhile. The project, which aimed to create one of the world's largest data center clusters, faced significant opposition from local landowners and advocacy groups.

data_points.project_notes: The project was abandoned after a lower court voided rezoning approvals and QTS decided not to pursue further litigation. The Board of County Supervisors dropped its legal defense in April, and Compass Datacenters also abandoned its involvement.
